claim: The alarmone (p)ppGpp regulates diverse targets.
source: The alarmone (p)ppGpp regulates diverse targets, yet its target specificity and evolution remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader literature context and the study's motivation.

claim: Basal (p)ppGpp inhibits the purine salvage enzyme HPRT by sharing a conserved motif with its substrate PRPP.
source: Here, we elucidate the mechanism by which basal (p)ppGpp inhibits the purine salvage enzyme HPRT by sharing a conserved motif with its substrate PRPP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript, including crystal structures and kinetic analyses.

claim: HPRT regulation by (p)ppGpp varies across organisms and correlates with HPRT oligomeric forms.
source: Intriguingly, HPRT regulation by (p)ppGpp varies across organisms and correlates with HPRT oligomeric forms.
evidence: This is supported by the biochemical survey of HPRT homologs and size exclusion chromatography data showing different oligomeric states.

claim: (p)ppGpp-sensitive HPRT exists as a PRPP-bound dimer or an apo- and (p)ppGpp-bound tetramer.
source: (p)ppGpp-sensitive HPRT exists as a PRPP-bound dimer or an apo- and (p)ppGpp-bound tetramer, where a dimer-dimer interface triggers allosteric structural rearrangements to enhance (p)ppGpp inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography, crosslinking experiments, and dynamic light scattering data.

claim: A dimer-dimer interface triggers allosteric structural rearrangements to enhance (p)ppGpp inhibition.
source: (p)ppGpp-sensitive HPRT exists as a PRPP-bound dimer or an apo- and (p)ppGpp-bound tetramer, where a dimer-dimer interface triggers allosteric structural rearrangements to enhance (p)ppGpp inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons and mutational analyses of the dimer-dimer interface.

claim: Loss of the oligomeric interface results in weakened (p)ppGpp regulation.
source: Loss of this oligomeric interface results in weakened (p)ppGpp regulation.
evidence: This is supported by data from loop II deletion variants and naturally occurring dimeric HPRTs.

claim: Protein oligomerization allows evolutionary change to accumulate away from a conserved binding pocket to allosterically alter specificity of ligand interaction.
source: Our results reveal an evolutionary principle whereby protein oligomerization allows evolutionary change to accumulate away from a conserved binding pocket to allosterically alter specificity of ligand interaction.
evidence: This is supported by ancestral sequence reconstruction and comparative analysis of HPRT homologs.

claim: This principle explains how another (p)ppGpp target GMK is variably regulated across species.
source: This principle also explains how another (p)ppGpp target GMK is variably regulated across species.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data on GMK variants with and without C-terminal tails.

claim: Most ligands bind near protein interfaces.
source: Since most ligands bind near protein interfaces, we propose that this principle extends to many other protein–ligand interactions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Gao and Skolnick, 2012) mentioned in the discussion.

claim: (p)ppGpp directly binds and regulates diverse protein targets at positions ranging from protein active sites to protein–protein interfaces.
source: (p)ppGpp directly binds and regulates diverse protein targets at positions ranging from protein active sites to protein–protein interfaces (Corrigan et al., 2016; Gourse et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2015a; Sherlock et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: How diverse themes of (p)ppGpp regulation evolve across bacterial species have not been systematically elucidated.
source: However, how these diverse themes evolve across bacterial species have not been systematically elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: (p)ppGpp at basal levels has important protective roles.
source: In addition, while most of the (p)ppGpp regulation is studied for high (p)ppGpp concentrations upon stress and starvation (Cashel et al., 1996; Gourse et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2015a), (p)ppGpp at basal levels also has important protective roles (Gaca et al., 2013; Gaca et al., 2015a; Kriel et al., 2012; Potrykus et al., 2011; Puszynska and O'Shea, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Molecular targets and mechanisms of basal (p)ppGpp regulation have not been delineated.
source: However, molecular targets and mechanisms of basal (p)ppGpp regulation have not been delineated.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: HPRT is one of the earliest identified targets of (p)ppGpp.
source: Here, we examined the specificity of (p)ppGpp binding by characterizing (p)ppGpp regulation of the enzyme hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT), one of the earliest identified targets of (p)ppGpp (Hochstadt-Ozer and Cashel, 1972; Kriel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HPRT is a purine salvage enzyme that converts purine bases and PRPP to GMP and IMP.
source: HPRT is a purine salvage enzyme that converts purine bases and PRPP to GMP and IMP, which are precursors of the essential nucleotide GTP (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This is a well-established biochemical fact about HPRT function, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: GMP and IMP are precursors of the essential nucleotide GTP.
source: HPRT is a purine salvage enzyme that converts purine bases and PRPP to GMP and IMP, which are precursors of the essential nucleotide GTP (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This is a well-established biochemical fact.

claim: HPRT activity was previously found to be inhibited by (p)ppGpp in several bacteria including Bacillus subtilis.
source: HPRT activity was previously found to be inhibited by (p)ppGpp in several bacteria including Bacillus subtilis (Gaca et al., 2015b; Hochstadt-Ozer and Cashel, 1972; Kriel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In B. subtilis, (p)ppGpp ranges from <30 μM at basal concentrations to millimolar levels upon starvation.
source: In B. subtilis, (p)ppGpp ranges from <30 μM at basal concentrations to millimolar levels upon starvation.
evidence: This is a statement about physiological (p)ppGpp concentrations, likely based on previous literature.

claim: (p)ppGpp inhibits B. subtilis HPRT activity at an IC50 of ≈10 μM.
source: (p)ppGpp inhibits B. subtilis HPRT activity at an IC50 of ≈10 μM, allowing (p)ppGpp to regulate purine salvage at its basal concentrations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the inhibition curve shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The absence of (p)ppGpp in B. subtilis results in an uncontrolled GTP increase and toxicity upon guanine addition.
source: The absence of (p)ppGpp in B. subtilis results in an uncontrolled GTP increase and toxicity upon guanine addition (Kriel et al., 2012) (Figure 1A, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: E. coli XGPRT is more weakly inhibited by pppGpp than B. subtilis HPRT.
source: E. coli XGPRT more weakly inhibited by pppGpp than B. subtilis HPRT. The IC50 for E. coli XGPRT is 45 µM compared to 10 µM for B. subtilis HPRT.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of E. coli XGPRT leads to imbalanced GTP/ATP homeostasis in B. subtilis.
source: Expression of E. coli XGPRT leads to imbalanced GTP/ATP homeostasis in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is supported by the thin layer chromatography data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: pppGpp is a strong competitive inhibitor of PRPP for B. subtilis HPRT.
source: We performed Michaelis Menten kinetics on B. subtilis HPRT and found (p)ppGpp is a strong competitive inhibitor of its substrate PRPP (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The Ki for pppGpp is 1.7 μM for B. subtilis HPRT.
source: The Ki for pppGpp is 1.7 μM, while the Km for PRPP is 166 μM, allowing (p)ppGpp at a basal level to effectively compete with physiological concentrations (0.1–1 mM) of PRPP (Bennett et al., 2009; Hove-Jensen et al., 2017) and keep GTP under surveillance not just during starvation, but also during unstarved growth.
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data and comparison with physiological PRPP concentrations.

claim: The Km for PRPP is 166 μM for B. subtilis HPRT.
source: The Ki for pppGpp is 1.7 μM, while the Km for PRPP is 166 μM, allowing (p)ppGpp at a basal level to effectively compete with physiological concentrations (0.1–1 mM) of PRPP (Bennett et al., 2009; Hove-Jensen et al., 2017) and keep GTP under surveillance not just during starvation, but also during unstarved growth.
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data.

claim: Physiological concentrations of PRPP are 0.1–1 mM.
source: The Ki for pppGpp is 1.7 μM, while the Km for PRPP is 166 μM, allowing (p)ppGpp at a basal level to effectively compete with physiological concentrations (0.1–1 mM) of PRPP (Bennett et al., 2009; Hove-Jensen et al., 2017) and keep GTP under surveillance not just during starvation, but also during unstarved growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Conservation of HPRT binding to (p)ppGpp is limited within distinct bacterial phyla for RNA polymerase and guanylate kinase.
source: It has been shown for the (p)ppGpp targets RNA polymerase and guanylate kinase that conservation of their binding to (p)ppGpp is limited within distinct bacterial phyla (Liu et al., 2015b; Ross et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: (p)ppGpp can bind and inhibit activities of HPRTs from every phylum of bacteria tested, including Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Deinococcus-Thermus, and Proteobacteria, and even eukaryotic HPRTs.
source: We revealed (p)ppGpp can bind and inhibit activities of HPRTs from every phylum of bacteria we tested, including Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Deinococcus-Thermus, and Proteobacteria, and even eukaryotic HPRTs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the biochemical survey data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most HPRTs were strongly inhibited by ppGpp and pppGpp at 25 μM.
source: To do so, we purified 32 recombinant HPRTs and tested their enzymatic activities and found that most of them were strongly inhibited by ppGpp and pppGpp at 25 μM (Figure 2A–B and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in Figure 2A-B and Table 1.

claim: (p)ppGpp is induced to millimolar concentrations during starvation in B. subtilis and E. coli.
source: Considering that (p)ppGpp is induced to millimolar concentrations during starvation and its uninduced levels are ≈10–30 μM during exponential growth in B. subtilis and E. coli (Cashel et al., 1996; Kriel et al., 2012), these results suggest significant inhibition of HPRT under physiological, basal levels of (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Uninduced levels of (p)ppGpp are ≈10–30 μM during exponential growth in B. subtilis and E. coli.
source: Considering that (p)ppGpp is induced to millimolar concentrations during starvation and its uninduced levels are ≈10–30 μM during exponential growth in B. subtilis and E. coli (Cashel et al., 1996; Kriel et al., 2012), these results suggest significant inhibition of HPRT under physiological, basal levels of (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most HPRTs bind pppGpp with Kd values ranging from ≈0.1 to ≈10 μM.
source: Using this method, we found that most HPRTs bind pppGpp with Kd values ranging from ≈0.1 to ≈10 μM (Figure 2D and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: HPRTs from human microbiota commensals manifested the tightest interactions with pppGpp (Kd ≈ 0.1–1 μM).
source: HPRTs from human microbiota commensals, including all species from Bacteroidetes along with the Firmicutes Eubacterium spp. and Ruminococcus spp., manifested the tightest interactions with pppGpp (Kd ≈ 0.1–1 μM) (Figure 2D and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: A few HPRTs were only weakly inhibited by 25 μM (p)ppGpp.
source: Interestingly, a few HPRTs were only weakly inhibited by 25 μM (p)ppGpp (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Weakly regulated HPRTs all clustered in β- and γ-Proteobacteria, with the exception of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: These weakly regulated HPRTs all clustered in β- and γ-Proteobacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Neisseria meningitidis), with the exception of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis and binding data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Several bacterial HPRTs that were weakly inhibited by 25 μM pppGpp are also almost refractory to high concentration of pppGpp.
source: However, several bacterial HPRTs that were weakly inhibited by 25 μM pppGpp (e.g. C. burnetii, L. pneumophila) are also almost refractory to high concentration of pppGpp.
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All HPRTs in Bacteroidetes were potently inhibited by pppGpp but only weakly by ppGpp.
source: All HPRTs in Bacteroidetes were potently inhibited by pppGpp but only weakly by ppGpp (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Nearly all other HPRTs displayed stronger inhibition by ppGpp than pppGpp.
source: In contrast, nearly all other HPRTs displayed stronger inhibition by ppGpp than pppGpp.
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Bacteroides spp. contain a GppA homolog and make mostly ppGpp in vivo.
source: It is noted that Bacteroides spp., whose HPRTs are more sensitive to pppGpp than ppGpp, contain a GppA homolog, and they make mostly ppGpp in vivo (Glass et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Firmicutes lack GppA homologs and produce predominantly pppGpp.
source: On the other hand, Firmicutes, whose HPRTs are more sensitive to ppGpp than pppGpp, lack GppA homologs and produce predominantly pppGpp.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of bacterial (p)ppGpp metabolism.

claim: pppGpp competitively inhibits B. anthracis Hpt-1 similarly to B. subtilis HPRT.
source: To examine the molecular determinants underlying (p)ppGpp regulation of HPRT, we turned to Hpt-1 from the pathogenic bacterium B. anthracis, which pppGpp competitively inhibits similarly to B. subtilis HPRT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apo HPRT diffracted to 2.06 Å resolution with four molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: Apo HPRT diffracted to 2.06 Å resolution with four molecules in the asymmetric unit and was nearly identical to a deposited apo structure of B. anthracis Hpt-1 (PDB ID 3H83) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data.

claim: The HPRT-substrates structure diffracted to 1.64 Å containing two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: The HPRT-substrates structure diffracted to 1.64 Å containing two molecules in the asymmetric unit (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and PRPP and 9-deazaguanine were coordinated by two Mg2+ ions with each monomer (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data.

claim: The HPRT-ppGpp complex diffracted to 2.1 Å resolution with two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: The HPRT-ppGpp complex diffracted to 2.1 Å resolution with two molecules in the asymmetric unit (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and each monomer contained one ppGpp coordinated with Mg2+, in agreement with near 1:1 stoichiometry measured via ITC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data and ITC data.

claim: ppGpp binds the HPRT active site and closely mimics the conformation of the two substrates.
source: Comparison between the HPRT-ppGpp and HPRT-substrates structures revealed that ppGpp binds the HPRT active site and closely mimics the conformation of the two substrates (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The purine ring of ppGpp overlaps with the purine base substrate.
source: The purine ring of ppGpp overlaps with the purine base substrate, and the two phosphate arms of ppGpp and PRPP both spread across the active site between loop I and loop III (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The (p)ppGpp-binding site in HPRT manifests a novel (p)ppGpp–protein interaction.
source: The (p)ppGpp-binding site in HPRT manifests a novel (p)ppGpp–protein interaction.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known (p)ppGpp binding modes.

claim: This binding pocket illustrates the first example of a (p)ppGpp binding motif that shares the PRPP-binding motif.
source: In sum, this binding pocket illustrates the first example of a (p)ppGpp binding motif that shares the PRPP-binding motif.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis and comparison with known binding motifs.

claim: Most (p)ppGpp-interacting residues are highly conserved across bacteria.
source: A frequency logo of the binding pocket from 99 bacterial HPRTs shows that most (p)ppGpp-interacting residues are highly conserved across bacteria (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 8), and nearly all binding residues are also conserved in the eukaryotic HPRTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence logo shown in Figure 3F and the alignment in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: Nearly all (p)ppGpp binding residues are also conserved in eukaryotic HPRTs.
source: A frequency logo of the binding pocket from 99 bacterial HPRTs shows that most (p)ppGpp-interacting residues are highly conserved across bacteria (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 8), and nearly all binding residues are also conserved in the eukaryotic HPRTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by the alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: All residues involved in binding ppGpp are also involved in binding substrates.
source: Since all residues involved in binding ppGpp are also involved in binding substrates, altering the site to affect inhibitor binding would also impact enzyme activity.
evidence: This is based on the structural comparison of ppGpp-bound and substrate-bound HPRT.

claim: Apo B. subtilis HPRT is a tetramer.
source: Using size-exclusion chromatography, we confirmed that apo B. subtilis HPRT is a tetramer (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When PRPP is added at a high concentration (500 μM) in the mobile phase, HPRT tetramers dissociate to dimers.
source: In contrast, when PRPP, the first substrate to bind HPRT (Yuan et al., 1992), is added at a high concentration (500 μM) in the mobile phase, HPRT tetramers dissociate to dimers (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: pppGpp prevents PRPP-induced dimer–dimer dissociation.
source: Importantly, with both PRPP and pppGpp present, HPRT was tetrameric (Figure 4C, lanes 6 and 7 and Table 3), indicating that pppGpp prevents PRPP-induced dimer–dimer dissociation.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 4C and dynamic light scattering data in Table 3.

claim: pppGpp selectively stabilizes HPRT tetramers against PRPP-induced dissociation.
source: Thus, pppGpp appears to selectively stabilize HPRT tetramers against PRPP-induced dissociation.
evidence: This is based on the crosslinking and dynamic light scattering data.

claim: HPRT binds PRPP as catalytically active dimers.
source: Taken together, these data reveal that HPRT binds PRPP as catalytically active dimers, whereas (p)ppGpp maintains HPRT as tetramers.
evidence: This is based on the oligomerization and activity data.

claim: (p)ppGpp maintains HPRT as tetramers.
source: Taken together, these data reveal that HPRT binds PRPP as catalytically active dimers, whereas (p)ppGpp maintains HPRT as tetramers.
evidence: This is based on the oligomerization data.

claim: The dimer–dimer interaction is critical for HPRT's regulation by (p)ppGpp.
source: To understand the importance of HPRT's differential oligomeric state with substrates and (p)ppGpp, we performed interface mutational analyses, and we found that, unexpectedly, the dimer–dimer interaction is critical for HPRT's regulation by (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational analysis data.

claim: The tetrameric Δloop II (70-76) bound pppGpp as tightly as wild-type HPRT.
source: While the tetrameric Δloop II (70-76) bound pppGpp as tightly as wild-type HPRT, the dimeric Δloop II (69-77) displayed strongly ablated binding to pppGpp (Kd too weak to estimate; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The dimeric Δloop II (69-77) displayed strongly ablated binding to pppGpp.
source: While the tetrameric Δloop II (70-76) bound pppGpp as tightly as wild-type HPRT, the dimeric Δloop II (69-77) displayed strongly ablated binding to pppGpp (Kd too weak to estimate; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In nearly all cases, the (p)ppGpp-insensitive HPRTs were also constitutive dimers.
source: Strikingly, in nearly all cases, the (p)ppGpp-insensitive HPRTs were also constitutive dimers (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tetrameric HPRT, but not dimeric HPRT, allows (p)ppGpp at basal levels to bind to and inhibit its activity.
source: Our results suggest that tetrameric HPRT, but not dimeric HPRT, allows (p)ppGpp at basal levels to bind to and inhibit its activity.
evidence: This is based on the combined oligomerization and binding data.

claim: Loop II in dimeric L. pneumophila HPRT is positioned closer to the active site.
source: Loop II in dimeric L. pneumophila HPRT is positioned closer to the active site (Figure 5B), mimicking substrates-bound HPRT even in the absence of substrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and compresses the cavity surrounding the 5′ phosphates of ppGpp (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Bsu-Lpn chimera is a stable dimer.
source: The chimera is a stable dimer (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that the determinants for oligomerization lie in the dimer-dimer interface residues.
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The chimera had a > 20 fold lower affinity for pppGpp than the tetramer.
source: The chimera also had a > 20 fold lower affinity for pppGpp than the tetramer (Kd ≈ 24 μM versus ≈ 1 μM) (Figure 5E), and PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the dimeric chimera than to tetrameric WT (Figure 5F), suggesting that there may be an evolved linkage between the dimer–dimer interface of HPRT tetramers and (p)ppGpp regulation.
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the dimeric chimera than to tetrameric WT.
source: The chimera also had a > 20 fold lower affinity for pppGpp than the tetramer (Kd ≈ 24 μM versus ≈ 1 μM) (Figure 5E), and PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the dimeric chimera than to tetrameric WT (Figure 5F), suggesting that there may be an evolved linkage between the dimer–dimer interface of HPRT tetramers and (p)ppGpp regulation.
evidence: This is supported by the competition data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Anc1 HPRT was likely tetrameric.
source: Notably, Anc1 HPRT was likely tetrameric, since it lacks the residues found in the dimeric lineage (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on ancestral sequence reconstruction and comparison with extant sequences.

claim: Lys81 is highly conserved in (p)ppGpp-regulated HPRTs but not in (p)ppGpp-insensitive HPRTs.
source: Lys81 is highly conserved in (p)ppGpp-regulated HPRTs but not in (p)ppGpp-insensitive HPRTs (Figure 6B), suggesting that (p)ppGpp regulation is associated with the evolution of this residue.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: pppGpp bound less well to both K81A and K81E HPRT variants relative to wild-type HPRT.
source: Importantly, pppGpp bound less well to both K81A and K81E HPRT variants relative to wild-type HPRT (Figure 6D), and PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the K81A variant relative to the tetrameric wild type (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA binding data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the K81A variant relative to the tetrameric wild type.
source: Importantly, pppGpp bound less well to both K81A and K81E HPRT variants relative to wild-type HPRT (Figure 6D), and PRPP more potently competed with pppGpp binding to the K81A variant relative to the tetrameric wild type (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the competition data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The HPRT dimer-dimer interface has coevolved with strong (p)ppGpp regulation.
source: We conclude that the HPRT dimer-dimer interface has coevolved with strong (p)ppGpp regulation by sequestering loop II at the dimer–dimer interface and opening the active site for (p)ppGpp binding (Figure 7), whereas evolution of interface residues associated with losing this dimer-dimer interaction weakens (p)ppGpp regulation.
evidence: This is based on the combined evolutionary, structural, and biochemical data.

claim: GMK is inhibited by (p)ppGpp in multiple phyla of bacteria but not in Proteobacteria despite the fact (p)ppGpp binds the conserved active site.
source: We previously found that GMK is inhibited by (p)ppGpp in multiple phyla of bacteria but not in Proteobacteria despite the fact (p)ppGpp binds the conserved active site (Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMK, a lid domain opens the active site for (p)ppGpp binding through pulling of the lid by the C-terminal helix of the adjoining monomer in a GMK dimer.
source: In the (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMK, a lid domain opens the active site for (p)ppGpp binding through pulling of the lid by the C-terminal helix of the adjoining monomer in a GMK dimer (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the (p)ppGpp-insensitive E. coli GMK, the lid domain is closed, with the C-terminal helix from the adjoining monomer perhaps responsible for stabilizing the closed position.
source: In the (p)ppGpp-insensitive E. coli GMK, the lid domain is closed, with the C-terminal helix from the adjoining monomer perhaps responsible for stabilizing the closed position (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus of B. subtilis GMK led to weakened binding between B. subtilis GMK and pppGpp and reduced inhibitory effect on its enzymatic activity.
source: Remarkably, while these residues are away from the (p)ppGpp binding pocket of the adjoining monomer, their deletion led to weakened binding between B. subtilis GMK and pppGpp and reduced inhibitory effect on its enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA and activity data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus of E. coli GMK allowed a weak binding between E. coli GMK and pppGpp, and rendered E. coli GMK sensitive to pppGpp inhibition.
source: On the other hand, deleting the C-terminus of the (p)ppGpp-resistant E. coli GMK allowed a weak binding between E. coli GMK and pppGpp, and rendered E. coli GMK sensitive to pppGpp inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the DRaCALA and activity data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: The allosteric interaction between the lid domain and C-terminus of two adjoining GMK monomers is the determining factor for (p)ppGpp specificity.
source: This demonstrates that the allosteric interaction between the lid domain and C-terminus of two adjoining GMK monomers is the determining factor for (p)ppGpp specificity.
evidence: This is based on the C-terminal deletion data for GMK.

claim: (p)ppGpp-insensitive and (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs use different residues to form the interaction between the lid domain and the C-terminal helix.
source: Importantly, these (p)ppGpp-insensitive and (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs use different residues to form the interaction between the lid domain and the C-terminal helix (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 8E.

claim: (p)ppGpp-insensitive GMKs have a hydrophobic interaction between the lid domain and C-terminal tail.
source: (p)ppGpp-insensitive GMKs have a hydrophobic interaction between the lid domain and C-terminal tail, whereas (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs contain more charged residues at this interface.
evidence: This is based on the sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs contain more charged residues at the lid domain - C-terminal tail interface.
source: (p)ppGpp-insensitive GMKs have a hydrophobic interaction between the lid domain and C-terminal tail, whereas (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs contain more charged residues at this interface.
evidence: This is based on the sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: Ancestral protein reconstruction suggests that the last common ancestor (Anc1) of GMK is more similar to the (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs (Anc3).
source: Ancestral protein reconstruction suggests that the last common ancestor (Anc1) is more similar to the (p)ppGpp-sensitive GMKs (Anc3) (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is based on ancestral sequence reconstruction shown in Figure 8E.
